name: NoFap / semen retention

card.summary: Abstaining from masturbation or ejaculation for supposed looks, testosterone and confidence gains; the claimed benefits have not been shown in studies.
card.note: Medical authors describe the claimed benefits as unsubstantiated; researchers have documented distress linked to abstinence framing and a Dhat-like anxiety syndrome.

quick.overview:
NoFap and semen retention are two overlapping practices of deliberately avoiding masturbation or ejaculation. NoFap began in 2011 as an online self-help community aimed at quitting pornography and masturbation. In looksmaxxing circles, abstinence is promoted as a route to more confidence, energy and an improved appearance.

Published reviews describe the claimed benefits as unsubstantiated, and a 2024 survey of online ejaculation-training courses found no instructors with medical or mental-health credentials. A widely cited 2003 study on testosterone rising after seven days of abstinence was retracted in 2021.
quick.mechanism: Proponents propose that retaining semen conserves nutrients or hormones, raises testosterone, or restores dopamine sensitivity, and so improves mood, skin, jawline or attractiveness. No published study has demonstrated these effects for looks.
quick.risks: Researchers have analyzed distress tied to abstinence and relapse framing in NoFap communities, and a 2024 letter describes a Dhat-like syndrome in anti-masturbation groups. The practice itself involves no substance, but men's-health content on social media has been rated as largely inaccurate.

lead: NoFap is an online movement and community whose members try to stop pornography use and masturbation, and semen retention is the related practice of deliberately reducing or stopping ejaculation. [1][2] Wikipedia says NoFap was founded in June 2011 by Alexander Rhodes after a Reddit thread about a 2003 study claiming testosterone rose after seven days of abstinence, a study that was retracted in 2021. [3]

Members cite religious or moral reasons, self-improvement, and physical benefits such as energy, focus and sleep. [3] In looksmaxxing communities the practice is also discussed as a way to improve confidence, social behavior or appearance. [4][5]

Medical authors describe the claimed benefits as lacking evidence. A 2024 study of online ejaculation-training programs found courses promoted with unsubstantiated health claims, and an analysis of TikTok and Instagram found semen retention had the most impressions of the men's-health topics studied, with accuracy rated poor overall. [2][6] Pornography addiction and sex addiction are not recognized as diagnoses in the DSM-5-TR or ICD-11, according to Wikipedia. [3]
infobox: No studies found for appearance benefits

paras: NoFap started as a Reddit community and grew into a forum, positioned as support for people wanting to quit pornography and masturbation. Its scientific claims trace largely to the anti-pornography activist Gary Wilson, whose work a historian has described as pseudoscientific. [3]

Semen retention and NoFap are promoted on social media, and a 2024 study identified eleven online courses teaching ejaculation training, priced from $5 to $147 per week or $20 to $199 one-time. [2] Researchers described a social media environment of highly engaging short-form video in which men consult the internet for sexual health concerns. [7]

Proponents on looksmax.org describe NoFap as a general-purpose solution to confidence problems and frame abstinence as part of the blackpill worldview, while others argue semen retention makes the body more attractive. [4][5] Courses analyzed in 2024 claimed to improve erectile dysfunction, premature ejaculation, porn addiction, sexual performance anxiety, testosterone levels and depression. [2]
No studies found testing abstinence or semen retention for appearance. The 2003 study that helped spark the movement, which reported higher testosterone after seven days, was retracted in 2021. [3]

Related research includes a 2021 qualitative analysis of NoFap/PornFree forum posts, which found that commitment to abstinence framed as recovery and relapse was a major factor maintaining distress. [8] A 2024 letter describes Dhat syndrome, a semen-loss anxiety syndrome described mainly in South Asia, emerging in the United States from anti-masturbation semen-retention groups. [9] A 2007 study had earlier reported Dhat-like symptoms among white Britons. [10] A 2026 bibliometric analysis mapped 3,239 articles on masturbation, noting contradictory positions between promoting it as healthy and linking it to negative experiences. [11]

Wikipedia reports that psychologist David Ley calls NoFap ideas simplistic and reliant on weak science, and that medical professionals generally attribute members' struggles to other mental health issues. [3] A 2025 narrative review and a 2024 social media analysis both characterize men's-health content online as frequently inaccurate, with physician posts rated more accurate than non-physician posts. [6][7]
On looksmax.org, threads range from posts calling NoFap key to success to posts arguing it has no effect, and members debate whether abstinence is a looksmaxxing tool or a distraction. [4][5][12]

timeline.event: A study reporting higher testosterone after seven days of abstinence is published; it was retracted in 2021. [3]
Alexander Rhodes founds NoFap in June. [3]
Qualitative analysis of NoFap forum data published; the 2003 study is retracted. [3][8]
Studies of ejaculation-training courses and Dhat syndrome in semen-retention groups appear. [2][9]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, NoFap and semen retention appear both as endorsed self-improvement practices and as targets of skepticism. [4][5][12]

claims.claim: Abstaining from masturbation improves confidence and success in life.
claims.believers: Posters describe NoFap as a key to success and as a response to problems such as race or height-related insecurity. [4][12]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that the most prominent claimed benefits lack evidence and that prolonged abstinence might worsen mental health problems; researchers found commitment to abstinence maintained distress in forum members. [3][8]

claims.claim: Semen retention forces the body to make itself more attractive.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread argues retention redirects the body toward attractiveness. [5]
claims.experts: No published study has tested semen retention for appearance. A 2024 review of online courses found the health claims unsubstantiated. [2]

claims.believers: Proponents point to a 2003 study reporting a testosterone rise after seven days. [3]
claims.experts: That study was retracted in 2021, and ejaculation-training courses claiming testosterone gains were noted by authors as not evidence-based. [2][3]

claims.believers: Other posters say a long streak changed nothing in their confidence or life. [12]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes prolonged abstinence might worsen mental health problems, and a 2024 letter describes semen-retention anxiety syndrome in these groups. [3][9]
